content:
Doris "Dorie" Miller (1919-1943) was an African American sailor who became a hero during the Pearl Harbor attack and a powerful symbol of courage and the fight for racial equality in the U.S. military.

## Early Life
- Born October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas
- Son of sharecroppers Henrietta and Connery Miller
- Named "Doris" after the midwife who delivered him, though he went by "Dorie"
- Was a fullback on his high school football team

## Naval Service
- Enlisted in the U.S. Navy in 1939 as a Mess Attendant Third Class
- At the time, African Americans in the Navy were restricted to serving as mess attendants, cooks, and stewards
- Was assigned to the USS West Virginia (BB-48) in 1940
- Known for his physical strength and boxing prowess aboard ship

## Pearl Harbor Heroism (December 7, 1941)
- During the attack, Miller was collecting laundry when the first bombs fell
- He helped move wounded sailors to safety, including the ship's mortally wounded captain, Mervyn Bennion
- Despite having no formal training, Miller manned a .50 caliber anti-aircraft gun and fired at attacking Japanese planes
- He remained at his post until ordered to abandon ship due to fires and flooding
- His actions were witnessed by multiple officers

## Recognition and Legacy
- Became the first African American to receive the Navy Cross (May 27, 1942)
- Admiral Chester Nimitz personally presented the award
- His heroism became a rallying point for civil rights advocates pushing for integration of the armed forces
- Toured the U.S. promoting war bonds

## Later Service and Death
- Promoted to Cook Third Class in 1942
- Assigned to the escort carrier USS Liscome Bay
- Killed in action on November 24, 1943, when the ship was torpedoed by a Japanese submarine during the Battle of Makin
- He was 24 years old

## Honors and Memorials
- USS Miller (FF-1091), a Knox-class frigate, was named in his honor (1973)
- USS Doris Miller (CVN-81), a future Ford-class aircraft carrier, will bear his name
- Multiple schools, parks, and buildings named after him
- Featured on a U.S. postage stamp
- His story has been depicted in numerous films, including "Pearl Harbor" (2001)

Miller's heroism challenged racial stereotypes and helped pave the way for greater opportunities for African Americans in the military. His actions demonstrated that courage and patriotism transcend racial boundaries, making him an enduring symbol of American valor and the struggle for equality.
